concepts.name: Chronology and periodization
concepts.summary: Place major events and eras such as prehistory, antiquity, medieval, early modern and modern in correct order using BCE/CE dating.

concepts.name: Neolithic agricultural revolution
concepts.summary: Explain how the shift from foraging to farming enabled settled communities and population growth.

concepts.name: River valley civilizations
concepts.summary: Describe how Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley and the Yellow River developed cities, irrigation and writing.

concepts.name: Classical Greece and Rome
concepts.summary: Outline key features of Greek city-states, Athenian democracy, the Roman Republic and Empire.

concepts.name: Early Chinese and Indian states
concepts.summary: Recall major dynasties and empires such as Qin, Han, Maurya and Gupta and their main achievements.

concepts.name: World religions' origins
concepts.summary: Explain where and when Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity and Islam arose and their central ideas.

concepts.name: Primary and secondary sources
concepts.summary: Distinguish evidence created in the period from later accounts written about it.

misconceptions.text: Ancient peoples were primitive and less intelligent than modern people.
Civilizations developed in isolation without contact or exchange.
Farming made life clearly better for everyone who adopted it.

concepts.name: Fall of Rome and successor states
concepts.summary: Describe the causes of Western Roman decline and the Byzantine, Islamic and Germanic kingdoms that followed.

concepts.name: Islamic caliphates and learning
concepts.summary: Explain the expansion of Islamic rule and its contributions in science, mathematics and trade.

concepts.name: Feudalism and medieval Europe
concepts.summary: Apply the ideas of lordship, vassalage and manorial economy to explain medieval European society.

concepts.name: Silk Road exchange networks
concepts.summary: Use examples of goods, ideas and diseases to show how trade routes linked Afro-Eurasia.

concepts.name: Mongol Empire and its effects
concepts.summary: Explain the Mongol conquests and their consequences for trade, politics and the spread of the Black Death.

concepts.name: Pre-Columbian Americas and Africa
concepts.summary: Describe major states such as Aztec, Inca, Mali and Songhai and their economies.

concepts.name: Cause and effect in history
concepts.summary: Apply short-term versus long-term cause and consequence to a given event.

misconceptions.text: The Middle Ages were a uniformly backward 'Dark Age' with no progress.
Rome fell suddenly in 476 CE and the whole empire ended then.
The Mongols were only destructive and contributed nothing to connections between regions.

concepts.name: Renaissance and Reformation
concepts.summary: Analyse how humanism, printing and religious conflict reshaped European thought and politics.

concepts.name: Early modern gunpowder empires
concepts.summary: Compare how the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal and Chinese empires built and legitimized power.

concepts.name: Columbian Exchange and Atlantic world
concepts.summary: Analyse the biological, economic and demographic impacts of European contact with the Americas and the Atlantic slave system.

concepts.name: Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment
concepts.summary: Apply Enlightenment ideas of reason, rights and natural law to explain political change.

concepts.name: Age of revolutions
concepts.summary: Compare the causes, ideologies and outcomes of the American, French, Haitian and Latin American revolutions.

concepts.name: Industrialization and its consequences
concepts.summary: Analyse why industrialization began in Britain and how it changed economies, cities and class relations.

concepts.name: Source analysis and corroboration
concepts.summary: Analyse a primary source's origin, purpose and audience and cross-check it against other evidence.

misconceptions.text: The Renaissance was a sudden break with the medieval period.
Revolutions always achieved liberty and equality for all people.
Industrialization was an inevitable result of European superiority.

concepts.name: Imperialism and colonial economies
concepts.summary: Analyse economic, ideological and strategic drivers of 19th-century imperialism and its extractive systems.

concepts.name: Responses to Western dominance
concepts.summary: Evaluate reform, resistance and adaptation strategies in Japan, China, India and the Ottoman Empire.

concepts.name: Origins of the world wars
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing explanations for the outbreak of World War I and the failures of the interwar settlement leading to World War II.

concepts.name: Totalitarianism and genocide
concepts.summary: Analyse how totalitarian regimes arose and enabled mass violence including the Holocaust.

concepts.name: Cold War global conflict
concepts.summary: Evaluate the Cold War's ideological and strategic dynamics and its effects on the decolonizing world.

concepts.name: Decolonization movements
concepts.summary: Analyse the varied paths to independence in India, Africa and Southeast Asia and their legacies.

concepts.name: Historiographical schools
concepts.summary: Evaluate how different schools of interpretation shape explanations of the same historical events.

misconceptions.text: World War I was caused solely by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand.
Colonized peoples were passive recipients of imperial rule.
The Cold War was only a US-Soviet conflict with little effect on the rest of the world.

concepts.name: Global and comparative history methods
concepts.summary: Evaluate comparative, connected and world-systems frameworks for their strengths and blind spots across regions.

concepts.name: Debating the Great Divergence
concepts.summary: Assess rival explanations for why industrial growth diverged between Europe and Asia.

concepts.name: Eurocentrism and periodization critique
concepts.summary: Critique how conventional periodization and narratives embed Eurocentric assumptions.

concepts.name: Memory, politics and commemoration
concepts.summary: Evaluate how states and societies use history in national narratives, memorials and education.

concepts.name: Environmental and big history
concepts.summary: Judge how climate, disease and ecological change act as long-run historical forces.

concepts.name: Designing an original historical argument
concepts.summary: Construct an original, evidence-based thesis using multilingual or varied archival sources and engaging prior scholarship.

concepts.name: Counterfactual and causal reasoning
concepts.summary: Create disciplined counterfactual arguments to weigh contingency against structural causes.

misconceptions.text: A single global narrative can be neutral and free of perspective.
Counterfactuals are idle speculation with no scholarly value.
Using more sources automatically makes a historical argument stronger.
